newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Enterprise gains as results impress.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Enterprise gains as results impress.

text.p: Shares in Enterprise Oil Plc climbed nearly three percent on Thursday as Britain's largest exploration and production firm released 1996 results which showed it has laid the foundations for solid growth.
Profit after tax rose 40 percent to 142.5 million sterling ($228.8 million) from 101.6 million sterling due to higher crude oil prices and increased production.
Last year's earnings were actually lower than most analysts had forecast, but the stock market was pleased the dividend was raised by a penny to 17.0 pence.
The figure that pleased most, however, was the low average finding cost of 99 pence per barrel of oil equivalent.
Together with reserve additions of 160 million barrels and a production replacement of 193 percent, Enterprise's future was looking bright, analysts said.

"You've got a high level of reserve replacement at a very cost effective level," said Colin Smith at BZW. "It basically means you're building in long-term profitable growth in the business," he added.
Enterprise also boosted investor confidence by saying it expected its 1999 production to be 320,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day (boepd) rather than the 300,000 previously forecast.
Average output in 1996 rose three percent to 242,932 boepd.
Recent discoveries in the UK and Italy prompted Enterprise to review its output estimate.
Besides Britain and Italy, Enterprise is also active in Denmark, and Norway, while it is also working hard to make the Gulf of Mexico a new core area.
The company's shares, which were last year's best performing blue chips on the London exchange, rose 18-1/2 pence to 652 in late afternoon trade.
Several other shares in the oil sector fell as Enterprise's new chief executive, Pierre Jungels, poured cold water on recent rumours Enterprise was preparing itself for a major acquisition.
Bid hopes had flared up after a weekend press report said Enterprise might make an acquisition this year of up to one billion sterling.
Monument Oil and Gas Plc was mentioned as a potential target as was British-Borneo, which also has promising operations in the Gulf of Mexico.
But Jungels said Enterprise was not interested in either company and added chances of an acquisition in 1996 were no bigger than in previous years.
British-Borneo consequently fell 12-1/2 pence to 1,410, while Monument retreated three pence to 82-3/4.
Jungels, meanwhile, sang the praises of Enterprise's high quality and relatively low risk assets.

Jungels, who took over the helm from current chairman Graham Hearne in January, said Enterprise had an advantage over many rivals in that it was not plagued by political unrest or major environmental headaches in the countries where it is operating.
The company also had the benefit of being only slightly involved in natural gas, where persistent oversupply has depressed prices, the new chief executive said.
The combination of good assets and highly skilled staff is "the guarantee that we can reproduce the performance of the past two years on a consistent basis," Jungels said. ($1=.6228 Pound)
